TESLA SAFETY IS THE NEW STANDARD — AND THE DATA PROVES IT

Tesla doesn’t just build electric cars. It builds some of the safest vehicles ever put on the road, and the numbers back it up year after year.

Here’s why Tesla has become the safety benchmark:

•Perfect NHTSA 5-Star Ratings — Every current Tesla model (Model 3, Y, S, X, Cybertruck) earns the highest possible 5-star overall rating, plus 5 stars in every subcategory: frontal crash, side crash, and rollover.
•Lowest Probability of Injury — According to NHTSA data, Tesla vehicles have the lowest probability of injury of any car sold in the United States.
•Real-World Crash Reduction — Tesla’s quarterly safety reports consistently show vehicles with Autopilot engaged have crash rates 5–10× lower than the U.S. national average. Full Self-Driving vehicles are pushing that number even further.
•Built-in Safety Features as Standard — Automatic Emergency Braking, Forward Collision Warning, Blind Spot Monitoring, 360° vision, and structural engineering that exceeds traditional safety standards are included on every vehicle — no extra cost.
•Continuous Improvement — Over-the-air updates regularly add new safety features and refine existing ones across the entire fleet. Safety gets better even after you buy the car.

Tesla’s approach is simple: use the best sensors, best software, best structural engineering, and constant data feedback to make cars dramatically safer than anything that came before.

Safety isn’t a marketing slogan at Tesla. It’s math, engineering, and relentless iteration.

The industry is now being forced to catch up.

Would you feel safer in a Tesla with Autopilot/FSD compared to a traditional gas car? Or do you still prefer human drivers for now?

WHY ELON MUSK AND SPACEX ARE GOING BACK TO THE MOON — AND WHY IT MATTERS

Elon Musk and SpaceX aren’t treating the Moon as the final destination.
 They see it as the essential stepping stone and high-fidelity rehearsal that makes Mars realistic, safer, and faster to achieve.

Here’s why the Moon is such a big priority right now:
•Orbital refueling must be proven The Moon is the first real destination that requires full ship-to-ship propellant transfer in orbit. It’s a much shorter, lower-risk mission than Mars, so SpaceX can test, fail, learn, and iterate quickly.
•Faster feedback loops Moon launch windows open multiple times per year. Mars windows are only every ~26 months. This means 5–10× more real flight tests of refueling, landings, ISRU, and reusability.
•Shared environmental challenges Vacuum, low gravity, abrasive regolith dust, radiation, extreme thermal cycles — the Moon has nearly every Mars-like hazard, but it’s close enough for quick aborts and immediate data return.
•ISRU & surface systems validation Turning lunar ice into propellant, extracting oxygen from regolith, deploying solar power in near-constant sunlight at the south pole — these must be proven at scale on the Moon before attempting them on Mars.
•NASA Artemis contracts Starship HLS is the official Human Landing System. Real money and hard deadlines are accelerating development while forcing reliability.
Elon has been clear about the strategy:
“The Moon is a great place to test the systems needed for Mars. It’s close enough to Earth to make it much easier to recover from failures, and it has many of the same challenges… Success on the Moon greatly increases the probability of success on Mars.”
The Moon isn’t the goal. It’s the fastest, safest on-ramp to Mars — and the key to making humanity multiplanetary in our lifetimes.
Which Moon milestone are you most excited for? First uncrewed Starship landing? Crewed Artemis landing? Lunar propellant production? Or a permanent south pole base?
